title: Gas State

Gaseous state is the form of matter in which the intermolecular distance between two molecules is very high, i.e. the molecules are very loosely packed.
1) Gases do not have a fixed shape, size, or definite volume. However, they take the shape of the container in which they are stored.
2) Gaseous molecules, or simply gases, expand on increasing temperature and condense on decreasing temperature.
3) Gases show diffusion (फैलाव) — from higher concentration to lower concentration.
4) Gases exert pressure on the wall of the container.

The temperature of gas is represented in the form of Kelvin (K). However, it can also be represented in the form of degree Celsius. But during calculation, the degree Celsius should be converted into the form of Kelvin (K).
Postulates of the Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
1) Gases consist of tiny particles called gas molecules.
2) Gas molecules are identical, having the same shape and size.
3) There is no (negligible) force of attraction between the gas molecules.
4) The volume of one gas molecule is negligible over the total volume occupied by the gas molecules.
5) The kinetic energy (KE) of gas molecules depends on the temperature of the gas.
6) The gas molecules are not stationary; they are not stable at any fixed position.
7) Gas molecules are in random motion, moving in a zig-zag pathway.
8) Collisions between gas molecules, and between gas molecules and the container wall, are perfectly elastic collisions — kinetic energy is preserved (conserved) during collision.

Graph 3 — PV vs P (same gas): Since $PV = k$ is constant regardless of P, plotting PV against P gives a straight horizontal line.
What it shows: the x-axis is Pressure (P), the y-axis is the product PV. The flat horizontal line confirms PV stays constant ($=k$) at all pressures — the clearest visual confirmation of Boyle's Law.

According to Charles' Law: $V \uparrow \; T \uparrow$ (as temperature increases, volume increases), and $V \downarrow \; T \downarrow$ (as temperature decreases, volume decreases) — at constant pressure.
Graphical Representation of Charles' Law and Absolute Temperature

What it shows: the x-axis is Temperature (in °C), the y-axis is Volume (V). The dashed portion is an extrapolation (gases would liquefy before actually reaching this point), while the solid line is the observed real-gas behavior. Clearly, from the graph, we can see that the volume of gas becomes zero (0) at a temperature of $-273.15°C$, or $0\,K$. This temperature is known as absolute temperature. At this temperature, the kinetic energy of gaseous molecules theoretically becomes equal to zero; however, practically this is not possible.

These graphs were introduced by Charles. Later on, Lord Kelvin proposed a new scale called the Kelvin scale of temperature by taking the information from Charles' Law — setting $0\,K$ at $-273.15°C$, the point where extrapolated gas volume reaches zero.
